mission.display_title: State conditions under which random variables are independent

knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 2.2.2
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly gives a clear independence condition for X and Y using joint and marginal language?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Independence is joint factorisation into marginals, or an equivalent CMP form.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Joint equals product of marginals on the support (or equivalent conditional-equals-marginal form).
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Skipping the factorisation hinge or confusing independence with weaker association summaries.

choices.label: X and Y are independent if the joint equals the product of the marginals for all (x, y) in the support (or an equivalent form such as conditional equals marginal).
X and Y are independent whenever their covariance is defined, even if the joint does not factor into marginals.
Independence means the joint equals the sum of the marginals for all (x, y).
Independence requires only that each marginal exists; the joint need not equal the product of those marginals.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 2.2.2
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. A student says correlation is zero, so X and Y are independent. Which statement is correct?
knowledge_checks.body: Refuse the claim; state the stronger warrant.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Uncorrelated does not imply independent; independence needs the joint factorisation warrant.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Refuse equating zero correlation with independence; require joint factorisation or equivalent.

choices.label: Refuse: zero correlation is not independence. Independence requires joint factorisation (or equivalent). Uncorrelated is weaker and can fail under nonlinear dependence.
Accept: zero correlation is necessary and sufficient for independence in all bivariate settings.
Refuse independence language entirely, and treat zero correlation as proving the joint cannot factor.
Zero correlation is stronger than independence, so factorisation of the joint is unnecessary once corr(X,Y)=0.

worked_example.title: Test independence on a theft-fire joint table
worked_example.problem_statement: A household book records indicators (X, Y) with joint PMF P(0,0) = 0.50, P(0,1) = 0.10, P(1,0) = 0.20, P(1,1) = 0.20, where X = 1 if a theft claim occurs and Y = 1 if a fire claim occurs in the same year. Compute the marginals, check whether X and Y are independent, and refuse equating zero covariance with independence in general.
worked_example.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Form marginals, then compare each joint cell with the product of marginals.

steps.label: Form the marginals
steps.attempt_cue: Sum rows/columns for P(X) and P(Y).

steps.label: Check the factorisation
steps.attempt_cue: Compare P(0,0) with P(X=0)P(Y=0), and at least one other cell.
steps.explanation: Independence requires P(x,y) = P(X=x)P(Y=y) for every cell. Here P(X=0)P(Y=0) = 0.60×0.70 = 0.42, but P(0,0) = 0.50 ≠ 0.42, so X and Y are not independent.

steps.label: Refuse uncorrelated-as-independent
steps.attempt_cue: State why Cov = 0 would not finish the independence check in general.
steps.explanation: Zero covariance is necessary under independence when variances are finite, but it is not sufficient in general. Independence is the full joint factorisation, not a single covariance number.
steps.calculation: Independence = joint factorisation everywhere; Cov = 0 is not a general proof
steps.result: Refuse Cov=0 as a general independence proof

worked_example.final_answer: Marginals are P(X=0)=0.60, P(X=1)=0.40, P(Y=0)=0.70, P(Y=1)=0.30. Since 0.60×0.70 = 0.42 ≠ P(0,0) = 0.50, X and Y are not independent. Zero covariance would not by itself prove independence in general.
worked_example.common_pitfall: Declaring independence from a quick look at the table, or treating Cov(X, Y) = 0 as a general proof of independence without checking joint factorisation.
